pairs.analogy_a: Imagine a household thermostat that keeps a room at a comfortable 22 °C. The thermostat has a temperature sensor (sensor detection) that constantly measures the air temperature and compares it to a preset set point. When the temperature drops below the set point, the thermostat signals the furnace to turn on (corrective response); when it rises above, it triggers the air‑conditioner to cool (feedback loop). The system also anticipates sudden drafts from an open window or a sunny afternoon (external perturbation handling) and adjusts heating or cooling intensity accordingly, ensuring the indoor climate stays within a viable range despite outside weather changes. This closed loop mirrors biological homeostasis, where cells sense internal conditions, compare them to optimal levels, and launch corrective actions while buffering external fluctuations.

pairs.controlled_operation: B removes the explicit mention of handling external perturbations such as drafts or sunlight, thereby omitting one core facet while preserving the rest of the mapping.

pairs.analogy_a: A city’s water supply system works like a living organism’s homeostasis. Sensors placed throughout the network detect pressure and flow rates (sensor detection) and compare them to a desired set point. If pressure falls, pumps are activated (corrective response) to raise it; if it spikes, valves open to release excess water (feedback loop). The system also compensates for sudden demand spikes, like a stadium event, by rerouting water from storage tanks (external perturbation handling), keeping the overall supply within safe limits despite fluctuating usage.

pairs.analogy_a: Consider a smartphone’s battery‑management system as an analogy for homeostasis. The device constantly reads voltage (sensor detection) and compares it to an optimal charge level (set point). When the charge falls, the OS reduces background activity and boosts charging speed (corrective response). When the battery overheats, the system throttles CPU performance (feedback loop) to prevent damage, while also adjusting brightness in response to ambient light changes (external perturbation handling). All components work together to keep the phone operating within safe limits.

pairs.analogy_a: Human body temperature regulation is a literal instance of homeostasis. Thermoreceptors in the skin and brain (sensor detection) constantly monitor core temperature and compare it to the 37 °C set point. If the body cools, shivering muscles generate heat (corrective response) and blood vessels constrict (feedback loop). If it overheats, sweat glands release moisture and vessels dilate, dissipating heat. External factors like ambient temperature or wind are sensed and compensated for, keeping internal temperature within a narrow viable range.
pairs.analogy_b: City traffic flow management resembles homeostasis in an adjacent way. Sensors at intersections detect vehicle density (sensor detection) and compare it to an optimal flow set point. When congestion builds, traffic lights extend green phases on busy streets (corrective response) and adjust timing across the network (feedback loop). The system also reacts to sudden events such as accidents or weather changes (external perturbation handling) to keep overall traffic moving smoothly, though the relation is adjacent rather than literal.
pairs.controlled_operation: B replaces the literal physiological example with an adjacent urban‑planning example, preserving full coverage and sound mapping while increasing conceptual distance.

pairs.analogy_a: A car’s cruise control system offers an adjacent analogy to homeostasis. Speed sensors (sensor detection) read the vehicle’s velocity and compare it to the driver‑set speed (set point). If the car slows, the throttle is opened (corrective response); if it speeds up, the throttle is reduced (feedback loop). The system also compensates for hills or wind (external perturbation handling) by adjusting throttle pressure, preserving the same type of carrier—mechanical force—throughout.
pairs.analogy_b: Financial portfolio rebalancing provides a cross‑domain projection of homeostasis. Market monitors track asset performance (sensor detection) against a target risk‑return profile (set point). When equities outperform, the system sells a portion and buys bonds (corrective response); when bonds lag, it does the opposite (feedback loop). External shocks like economic news or geopolitical events (external perturbation handling) trigger multiple simultaneous adjustments across asset classes, currencies, and derivatives, shifting the carrier type from mechanical force to monetary value and involving several central type changes.
pairs.controlled_operation: B shifts the analogy from an adjacent mechanical domain (cruise control) to a cross‑domain financial domain, introducing multiple carrier/type changes while keeping coverage and mapping sound.
